title: Jeremiah 15:10–21
context: Jeremiah laments his birth and his isolation, and the LORD answers with promises of strength, interspersed with words about the nation’s exile whose addressee is not clearly marked. Jeremiah’s lament resumes: he delighted in God’s words, yet asks why his pain is perpetual and whether God will be like a deceitful brook. The LORD calls him to return, promising to restore him and make him a bronze wall, echoing his call in 1:18–19. Both traditions read the passage pastorally as shared ground about honest lament and God’s restoring grace.

verses.text: Woe is me, my mother, that you have borne me, a man of strife, and a man of contention to the whole earth! I have not lent, neither have men lent to me; yet every one of them curses me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah cries, “Woe is me, my mother, that you have borne me,” a man of strife to the whole land, cursed by all though he neither lent nor borrowed. His lament begins.

Arminian readers see an honest cry of a faithful servant.
verses.reformedNotes:
The lament resembles Jeremiah’s later cry in 20:14 and Job’s in Job 3; it is honest speech before God, not a renunciation of faith.

Reformed readers see a prophet bearing his calling’s cost. Both traditions read this pastorally as shared ground.

verses.text: The LORD said, “Most certainly I will strengthen you for good. Most certainly I will cause the enemy to make supplication to you in the time of evil and in the time of affliction.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD answers that he will surely strengthen Jeremiah for good and make his enemies plead with him in times of trouble. Comfort is given.

Arminian readers see God responding personally to his servant’s distress.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse is difficult, and translations render its first line in different ways, but its tone is reassuring.

Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness to his called servant. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God sustaining those he sends.

verses.text: Can one break iron, even iron from the north, and bronze?
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD asks whether anyone can break iron, iron from the north, and bronze. The image is of strength.

Arminian readers see a picture of unbreakable resolve, though its exact application is unclear.
verses.reformedNotes:
Interpreters differ on whether the iron refers to the northern enemy’s invincibility or to the strength God gives Jeremiah (compare 1:18; 15:20).

Reformed readers see God’s purposes as unbreakable. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hold the sense tentatively.

verses.text: I will give your substance and your treasures for a plunder without price, and that for all your sins, even in all your borders.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will give their wealth and treasures as plunder without price for all their sins throughout their borders. Loss is announced.

Arminian readers see consequences falling on the nation for its sins.
verses.reformedNotes:
The addressee seems to shift here to the people as a whole, though the transition is not marked; similar words appear in 17:3–4.

Reformed readers see judgment on national sin. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hold the speaker shift tentatively.

verses.text: I will make them to pass with your enemies into a land which you don’t know; for a fire is kindled in my anger, which will burn on you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
They will be taken with their enemies into an unknown land, for a fire is kindled in the LORD’s anger. Exile is foretold.

Arminian readers see the consequences of persistent sin reaching their climax in exile from the land.
verses.reformedNotes:
Like verse 13, these words seem addressed to the nation rather than to Jeremiah personally.

Reformed readers see God’s anger against sin. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note the uncertain addressee, holding the transition between verses 12 and 13 tentatively.

verses.text: LORD, you know. Remember me, visit me, and avenge me of my persecutors. You are patient, so don’t take me away. Know that for your sake I have suffered reproach.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah prays, “LORD, you know,” asking God to remember him, visit him, avenge him of his persecutors, and not take him away in God’s patience, for he suffers reproach for God’s sake. His lament resumes.

Arminian readers see honest pleading.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jeremiah appeals to God’s knowledge and to his own faithfulness.

Reformed readers see a servant committing his cause to God. Both traditions read this as shared ground about prayer under persecution.

verses.text: Your words were found, and I ate them. Your words were to me a joy and the rejoicing of my heart, for I am called by your name, LORD, God of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah recalls that when God’s words were found, he ate them, and they were his joy, for he is called by God’s name. Delight in God’s word marked his calling.

Arminian readers see joyful reception of God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes:
The image of eating God’s words expresses deep, personal reception.

Reformed readers see God’s word sustaining his servant. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground and treasure the verse as a picture of delight in Scripture.

verses.text: I didn’t sit in the assembly of those who make merry and rejoice. I sat alone because of your hand, for you have filled me with indignation.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah says he did not sit among merrymakers but sat alone because of God’s hand, filled with indignation. His calling isolated him.

Arminian readers see the personal cost of faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
The prophet’s loneliness results from the message he carries, not from personal failure.

Reformed readers see a servant set apart for God’s purpose. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the loneliness that faithful witness can bring, handled with pastoral sympathy.

verses.text: Why is my pain perpetual, and my wound incurable, which refuses to be healed? Will you indeed be to me as a deceitful brook, like waters that fail?
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah asks why his pain is perpetual and his wound incurable, and whether God will be to him “as a deceitful brook, like waters that fail.” The complaint is bold.

Arminian readers see honest lament in deep anguish.
verses.reformedNotes:
The image contrasts sharply with God as “the spring of living waters” (2:13). It is a cry of pain, not Jeremiah’s final word about God.

Reformed readers likewise hear lament. Both traditions read this pastorally as shared ground.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD says, “If you return, then I will bring you again, that you may stand before me; and if you take out the precious from the vile, you will be as my mouth. They will return to you, but you will not return to them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD answers, “If you return, then I will bring you again,” so Jeremiah may stand before him and be his mouth; the people must turn to him, not he to them. Restoration is offered.

Arminian readers see a call to repentance answered by restoring grace.
verses.reformedNotes:
God’s answer neither ignores nor condemns the lament but calls Jeremiah back to his calling.

Reformed readers see God’s grace restoring his servant. Both traditions read this as shared ground about repentance and restoration.

verses.text: I will make you to this people a fortified bronze wall. They will fight against you, but they will not prevail against you; for I am with you to save you and to deliver you,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will make Jeremiah a fortified bronze wall; the people will fight him but not prevail, for God is with him to save and deliver. The original promise is renewed.

Arminian readers see God’s faithfulness to his servant.
verses.reformedNotes:
The promise closely echoes 1:18–19, where God first made Jeremiah “bronze walls.”

Reformed readers see God keeping his word to the one he called. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about God’s protecting presence with those he sends.

verses.text: “I will deliver you out of the hand of the wicked, and I will redeem you out of the hand of the terrible.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD promises to deliver Jeremiah from the hand of the wicked and redeem him from the hand of the ruthless. The chapter ends in assurance.

Arminian readers see God’s saving care for his servant after his honest lament.
verses.reformedNotes:
The final words answer Jeremiah’s plea for vindication in verse 15.

Reformed readers see God’s redemption of his servant. Both traditions read this as shared ground and see the lament answered not with rebuke alone but with renewed promise.
